name: Heparin
summary: A rapidly acting parenteral anticoagulant that potentiates antithrombin III; fully reversible with protamine, making it the default when anticoagulation must be controllable.
mechanism: Binds antithrombin III via a unique pentasaccharide sequence, accelerating its inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa with roughly equal anti-IIa and anti-Xa activity.
pharmacodynamics: Dose-dependent anticoagulation monitored by aPTT (goal typically 1.5–2.5× control).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic and reticuloendothelial desulfation/depolymerization; no CYP

dosing.adult: ACS: IV bolus 80 units/kg then 18 units/kg/h continuous infusion, titrated to aPTT; VTE: IV bolus 80 units/kg then 18 units/kg/h
dosing.renalAdjustment: Reduce dose in renal impairment; monitor aPTT

safety.pregnancy: May be used in pregnancy (does not cross the placenta)
warnings: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (type II) with paradoxical thrombosis — monitor platelets
Bleeding — fully reversed by protamine sulfate
safety.overdose: Protamine sulfate (1 mg per ~100 units of heparin)

indications: Anticoagulation for surgery, hemodialysis, and ECMO
clinicalPearls: Rapid onset and offset make it ideal when anticoagulation must be started or stopped quickly.
Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin, unlike LMWH.
good: Acute settings needing titratable, fully reversible anticoagulation.
bad: Patients with HIT history or needing long-term outpatient anticoagulation.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
